Liz Magill :: Career :: 1988–1996: Legal career :: chunk_0002
From 1988 until 1992, Magill worked as a senior legislative assistant for United States Senator [Kent Conrad](/wiki/Kent_Conrad "Kent Conrad") of North Dakota.[[3]](#cite_note-uva_bio-3) Following law school, Magill worked as a [law clerk](/wiki/Law_clerk "Law clerk") for Judge [J. Harvie Wilkinson III](/wiki/J._Harvie_Wilkinson_III "J. Harvie Wilkinson III") on the [United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit](/wiki/United_States_Court_of_Appeals_for_the_Fourth_Circuit "United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit") from 1995 until 1996, and then worked as a clerk for [United States Supreme Court](/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States "Supreme Court of the United States") Justice [Ruth Bader Ginsburg](/wiki/Ruth_Bader_Ginsburg "Ruth Bader Ginsburg") from 1996 until 1997.[[4]](#cite_note-4) She also became a member of the [American Law Institute](/wiki/American_Law_Institute "American Law Institute").[[5]](#cite_note-5)

In 1997, Magill joined the faculty of the [University of Virginia School of Law](/wiki/University_of_Virginia_School_of_Law "University of Virginia School of Law"), where she worked for 15 years.[[6]](#cite_note-:4-6) A scholar of [administrative](/wiki/Administrative_law "Administrative law") and [constitutional law](/wiki/Constitutional_law "Constitutional law"), she was the Joseph Weintraub–Bank of America Distinguished Professor of Law, the Elizabeth D. and Richard A. Merrill Professor,[[6]](#cite_note-:4-6) and from 2009 to 2012, the school’s vice dean.[[3]](#cite_note-uva_bio-3)[[7]](#cite_note-:0-7)

From 2012 to 2019, Magill was dean of the law school at Stanford University, where she was also Richard E. Lang Professor of Law.[[8]](#cite_note-:2-8) In 2016, she was elected a fellow of the [American Academy of Arts and Sciences](/wiki/American_Academy_of_Arts_and_Sciences "American Academy of Arts and Sciences").[[9]](#cite_note-9)

In 2019 she returned to the University of Virginia, where she served as [provost](/wiki/Provost_(education) "Provost (education)") from 2019 to 2022.[[7]](#cite_note-:0-7)

The UAE lies between 22°30' and 26°10' north latitude and between 51° and 56°25′ east longitude. The coolest month is January, averaging 5.4 °C (41.7 °F). The record low temperature was −9.2 °C (15.4 °F) on January 13, 1876. The record high was 39.5 °C (103.1 °F) on July 20, 2004.
The record highest low temperature is 30.4 °C (86.7 °F), on August 11, 2013.[[104]](#cite_note-106)

Annual rainfall averages nearly 1,600 millimeters (63.0 in), with a wetter summer and a drier winter. Two organizations have attempted but failed to achieve soft landings: Israeli private space agency [SpaceIL](/wiki/SpaceIL "SpaceIL") with their [Beresheet](/wiki/Beresheet "Beresheet") spacecraft (2019), and Japanese company [ispace](/wiki/Ispace_(Japanese_company) "Ispace (Japanese company)")'s [Hakuto-R Mission 1](/wiki/Hakuto-R_Mission_1 "Hakuto-R Mission 1") (2023).

On 22 February 2024, Intuitive Machine's [*Odysseus*](/wiki/Intuitive_Machines_Nova-C#IM-1_mission "Intuitive Machines Nova-C") successfully landed on the Moon after taking off on a SpaceX [Falcon 9](/wiki/Falcon_9 "Falcon 9") liftoff on 15 February 2024 in a mission by [NASA](/wiki/NASA "NASA"), [SpaceX](/wiki/SpaceX "SpaceX"), and [Intuitive Machines](/wiki/Intuitive_Machines "Intuitive Machines"), marking the United States' first soft unmanned Moon landing in over 50 years and as the first successful landing of a [privately owned spacecraft](/wiki/Private_spaceflight "Private spaceflight") on the Moon.[[11]](#cite_note-space.com-11)[[12]](#cite_note-12) The lander broke a strut during landing and rested at an angle of 30° to the lunar surface and 18° to horizontal, with communications impaired.[[13]](#cite_note-13)[[14]](#cite_note-14) It operated until February 29, 2024.[[15]](#cite_note-15)

On 2 March 2025, [Firefly Aerospace](/wiki/Firefly_Aerospace "Firefly Aerospace")'s [Blue Ghost](/wiki/Blue_Ghost_Mission_1 "Blue Ghost Mission 1") lunar lander made the first fully successful commercial Moon landing after softly landing upright near [Mons Latreille](/wiki/Mons_Latreille "Mons Latreille") in [Mare Crisium](/wiki/Mare_Crisium "Mare Crisium"). Blue Ghost operated for 14 days, including 5 hours into the lunar night, marking it the longest commercial operations on the Moon until now. Part of NASA's [Commercial Lunar Payload Services](/wiki/Commercial_Lunar_Payload_Services "Commercial Lunar Payload Services") initiative, Firefly operated 10 NASA instruments aboard Blue Ghost. The mission concluded on 16 March 2025.[[16]](#cite_note-16)[[17]](#cite_note-nssdca-17)[[18]](#cite_note-18)
